content: Methylchloroisothiazolinone, also known as 5-chloro-2-methyl-4-isothiazolin-3-one, is a chemical preservative that belongs to the isothiazolinone group. It exhibits both antibacterial and antifungal properties, making it effective against a wide range of microorganisms, including gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, yeast, and fungi. This compound is commonly incorporated into water-based personal care products and cosmetics to prevent microbial growth. Beyond cosmetics, it is also utilized in industrial applications such as glue production, detergents, paints, fuels, and other manufacturing processes. When combined with methylisothiazolinone, methylchloroisothiazolinone is marketed under the registered trade name Kathon CG. It can also be formulated with other compounds, such as alcohols and long-chain organic substances, to enhance its preservative effects. Examples of such combinations include methylchloroisothiazolinone with ethylparaben, benzalkonium chloride, or 2-bromo-2-nitropropane-1,3-diol. The use of methylchloroisothiazolinone in cosmetics dates back to the 1970s. However, at high concentrations, it has been shown to cause chemical burns and is known to irritate the skin and mucous membranes. Due to these adverse effects, its use has been significantly reduced in most cosmetic products, particularly those that involve prolonged skin contact. In some cases, it is included in cosmetic creams and lotions designed for sensitive users, as its formulation can be adjusted to minimize irritation. In the United States, the maximum allowable concentration is 15 parts per million (ppm) for rinse-off products and 8 ppm for other types of cosmetics. There are safety concerns associated with methylchloroisothiazolinone. Like several other common cosmetic ingredients, it has been evaluated for potential carcinogenicity. Additionally, it is recognized as an allergen and may cause allergic reactions in susceptible individuals.
